introduction: Henry V's funeral leaves England mourning a conqueror while rival nobles struggle over the government of his young son. In France, English commanders try to preserve the conquests they inherited against Charles and the newly arrived Joan la Pucelle. Talbot's military reputation gives his countrymen confidence, but court disputes repeatedly threaten their ability to act together. As red and white roses become factional badges, the war abroad becomes inseparable from questions of family rank, authority and allegiance at home.

fullSynopsis.text: At Henry V's funeral, Gloucester and Winchester quarrel while messengers announce English losses in France and Talbot's capture. Gloucester, Protector of the young Henry VI, plans to inspect the Tower's weapons, but Winchester bars his entry. Their servants fight until the Mayor enforces peace. In France, Joan la Pucelle claims a divine mission to rescue her country, recognizes Charles despite an attempted disguise and defeats him in a trial of arms. Charles accepts her leadership. Talbot returns through a prisoner exchange, only to see Salisbury mortally wounded by French cannon fire. Joan drives back the English and relieves Orleans, fulfilling her immediate promise.

Talbot, Bedford and Burgundy retake Orleans by a surprise night assault. Talbot honours the dead Salisbury and accepts an invitation from the Countess of Auvergne, who intends to capture him. He defeats her trap by summoning soldiers kept ready outside and explains that his strength resides in his army. In London's Temple Garden, Richard Plantagenet and Somerset turn a legal disagreement into a factional quarrel: their supporters choose white and red roses. Somerset attacks Richard's family standing. The dying prisoner Mortimer traces a rival royal claim through his family and names Richard his heir, while warning him to proceed cautiously against the established Lancastrian kings.

Henry urges Gloucester and Winchester to reconcile as their servants again fight in London. They join hands, but Winchester privately disowns the settlement. Henry restores Richard's inheritance and creates him Duke of York before preparing to be crowned in France. Joan then gains entry to Rouen with soldiers disguised as market sellers and signals the French attack. Talbot and Burgundy recover the city the same day, while the dying Bedford lives long enough to see victory. Joan next persuades Burgundy to abandon England for his own country. At Paris, Henry rewards Talbot as Earl of Shrewsbury, but the rose quarrel spreads to the nobles' servants.

Henry is crowned in Paris. Talbot strips Fastolf of his Garter for earlier flight, and the king banishes him. Burgundy's letter announces his defection. When Vernon and Basset seek permission to fight over their rival badges, Henry forbids the quarrel and appoints York regent, ordering Somerset's cavalry to cooperate with him. Instead, their mutual hostility obstructs relief when Talbot is surrounded near Bordeaux. York blames Somerset for withholding horsemen; Somerset calls the enterprise reckless and says York could have requested the horsemen. Lucy appeals to both in vain. Somerset finally promises aid, but Lucy judges it too late.

Talbot urges his newly arrived son John to escape and preserve their family name. John refuses to desert him, even after his father rescues him in battle and renews the plea. Young Talbot dies fighting; his body is brought to his father, who dies holding him. Charles refuses a proposal to mutilate the bodies and allows Lucy to take them for burial. England subsequently pursues peace and a marriage between Henry and Armagnac's daughter. Winchester, now a cardinal, prepares to negotiate, but privately renews his ambition to dominate Gloucester. The French face a reunited English army, and Joan calls on fiends who appear but refuse her help.

York captures Joan. Condemned to burn, she denies the shepherd who claims her as his daughter, asserts noble and holy origins, then pleads pregnancy with changing accounts of the father. These claims do not save her: she is led away under guard with the execution order standing. Winchester brings Henry's peace commission. Charles reluctantly accepts subordinate rule under Henry and gives tokens of allegiance, while reserving his garrison towns. Meanwhile Suffolk captures Margaret and, attracted to her, arranges her proposed marriage to Henry with Reignier's consent and assurances about Maine and Anjou. Suffolk persuades Henry to abandon the earlier match. Henry commissions him to fetch Margaret; Suffolk privately intends to rule through her.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: The funeral of Henry V exposes conflict among the nobles responsible for the young Henry VI. Gloucester and Winchester quarrel even before successive messengers describe losses in France and Talbot's captivity. Their dispute becomes violence outside the Tower when Winchester's men deny the Protector entry. The Mayor imposes a temporary peace. Across the Channel, Charles receives Joan la Pucelle, who declares a heavenly mission, sees through his test of her recognition and beats him in combat. Talbot, released by exchange, rejoins Salisbury at Orleans. A cannon shot kills Gargrave and fatally wounds Salisbury as the English survey the city. Joan leads a successful French relief and enters Orleans despite Talbot's resistance. Charles celebrates her achievement and promises extraordinary honours.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Talbot, Bedford and Burgundy surprise the celebrating French and recover Orleans. Salisbury's body is brought into the town, where Talbot promises a commemorative tomb. Invited to the Countess of Auvergne's castle, Talbot finds that admiration masks an attempt to imprison him. His waiting soldiers enter at his signal, overturning the trap; he accepts hospitality rather than revenge. In England, Plantagenet and Somerset's dispute hardens into opposed factions marked by white and red roses. Taunts about his father's execution drive Plantagenet to question the imprisoned Mortimer. Mortimer recounts a rival claim to the crown through his family and identifies Richard as his heir before dying. Richard keeps the dynastic counsel private while preparing to seek restoration of his status in Parliament.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Gloucester and Winchester renew their accusations in Parliament while their servants fight with stones. Henry's appeals secure an outward reconciliation, but private comments reveal its weakness. Henry restores Plantagenet's blood and inheritance and makes him Duke of York. In France, Joan's soldiers enter Rouen as corn sellers, allowing a French seizure of the city. Talbot and Burgundy counterattack and recover it; the sick Bedford dies after witnessing the French retreat. Fastolf meanwhile openly chooses flight rather than help Talbot. Joan compensates for the defeat by persuading Burgundy to change sides through appeals to France's suffering and his own interests. Henry honours Talbot in Paris, but Vernon and Basset's quarrel shows the rose factions spreading among their followers.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: At Henry's French coronation, Talbot tears Fastolf's Garter away, and Henry banishes the disgraced knight. News of Burgundy's defection is followed by fresh demands for combat between the rose factions. Henry forbids their feud, wears Somerset's red rose while denying partiality, and makes York regent with orders for Somerset to supply cavalry. Talbot is then trapped by superior forces near Bordeaux. York and Somerset blame one another as Lucy begs them to send aid; their rivalry leaves Talbot unsupported. Talbot repeatedly urges his son John to escape, but John refuses to preserve himself at his father's expense. The young man dies in battle, and Talbot dies embracing his body. Charles allows Lucy to recover the dead for burial.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Henry supports peace and a proposed marriage to Armagnac's daughter, while Winchester's new cardinalship renews his private ambition. In France, Joan's summoned fiends refuse further aid, and York captures her. She is condemned to burn; her contradictory claims about birth, holiness and pregnancy fail to obtain mercy, and guards lead her away. Winchester negotiates Charles's qualified submission to Henry as part of a truce. Suffolk meanwhile captures Margaret, becomes attracted to her and negotiates her proposed marriage to Henry, promising Reignier security in Maine and Anjou. Back in England, his praise overcomes Gloucester and Exeter's objections about the previous betrothal and the new match's poor financial terms. Henry sends Suffolk to fetch Margaret, and Suffolk anticipates controlling the king through her.
